item.title: Are We in an Era of "Joyless Decadence"?
item.description:
Happiness

Are We in an Era of "Joyless Decadence"?

Michèle Mendelssohn and Charlie Tyson have named a new malaise afflicting modern life.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • "Being the best version of yourself" and "living your best life" are at best solipsistic.
  • The underlying competition in the games of optimizing and maxxing foment comparison, the thief of joy.
  • Joyless decadence is when people ceaselessly optimize yet remaining ultimately unsatisfied.
  • Happiness is an inside job.

"Comparison is the thief of joy." —Teddy Roosevelt

The second time I met Esther Perel, I told her that she was a tremendous poet. The musicality of her ingenious ditties such as "How can you desire what you already have?" render them instantly iconoclastic and deliciously memorable.

Similar is the case for Michèle Mendelssohn and Charlie Tyson's concept expressed recently in The Guardian defining our current malaise—the simmering low-level dysthymia of our epoch—with a poetic twist worthy of Rilke: joyless decadence. The term aims to capture our era of people ceaselessly optimizing and going to extremes to appear hip, cool, rich and sexy yet remaining ultimately unsatisfied.

Twenty years of private practice psychotherapy have taught me what the famous Harvard longitudinal study demonstrated: that the quality of our intimate relationships predicts happiness more reliably than any other variable researchers have measured—more reliably than income, achievement, and the outside appearance of the body we incarnate. Everyday I meet people who on the outside have attained enviable wealth and fame and yet feel dead inside.

The underlying competition in our social games of optimizing and maxxing—trying to take the coolest vacation, wear the coolest baseball hat, drive the coolest car, have the coolest shoes and handbags, and shop at the coolest stores—engender constant comparison. This measuring ourselves against others, against our family and friends even, is the thief of joy.

So there is ultra-decadence as reported on our screens every morning and yet there is little joy. Life feels flat even though we're walking our 10,000 steps and taking all of our supplements, and getting thousands of likes on social media.

I'll give you a hint as to where this is going: Ten years ago in "How To Survive Your Childhood Now That You’re An Adult,” I wrote “One hug equals one million LIKEs.” In my office, where people come to escape the competition of unceasingly performing their exclusive lifestyle's beauty and success at their local cafes and gyms (and videoing it), I hear about daily loneliness. It turns out that all of this decadence is rather solitary; this "being the best version of myself" and "living my best life" is at best solipsistic.

Ironically, even the optimizing of sensual pleasures—us gourmands—has grown increasingly joyless. The brief ecstasy of Erewhon's famous $25 strawberry (yes, one strawberry) is more about the competition to acquire one of these trophies than the actual 30 seconds of savoring it.

Mendelssohn and Tyson describe an elite that treats even sexual vitality as a competition, something gamified by Oura rings and Apple watches. They cite an OB-GYN who poetically branded her followers as the "Billionaire's Vagina Club"—women tracking their hormones for self-optimization, similar to the way many finance guys track and optimize their investment portfolios.

Y’see, joy is the real measure of the good life. You can have a large bank account and six-pack abs but neither correlate strongly scientifically with authentic happiness.

I took one of those "Navy Seal workout classes for rich people" in Brentwood last week. (It was a 10 am class, which suggested to me that nobody in the room had a 9-5 job.) It was an extremely rigorous exercise routine, and by the end of class my mat had the consistency of clam chowder. Like cultural anthropologist Margaret Mead, here's what I observed: 30 people depositing their Louis Vuitton, Vuori, and Erewhon sacks gently in the back of the room, namedropping recent travel victories, and adding in push-ups during resting periods, obviously trying to rival Matt Damon's biceps (that are really not his biceps, according to the NY Times). This to me is the joyless decadence of looksmaxxing and biohacking that will eventually land in my office as dysthymia. "I'm doing everything right—so why do I feel dead inside?"

How Did Our Culture Become So Misguided?

Yes, you might attract a higher status mate with a billion dollars in crypto or a vagina worthy of a billionaire, but will that mate have the emotional capability of making you feel loved? Or will they be too busy reading their sleep and ovulation scores and other bio-metrics to spend quality time looking you lovingly in your eyes or hugging you?

If you've taken my classes, you know that I believe America is a giant resentment factory and the optimization culture that Mendelssohn and Tyson describe in their articles is its engine. We are raised to believe that being liked is a matter of being impressive, that the body, the income, the gloss, and the glitz of our highly curated selves are the instruments of seduction that will make another person love us, so we spend our time performing an optimized persona instead of exposing our messy authentic selves to a cruel judgmental world. A dilemma: to be liked for who you are not or be left alone?

Trust me, only a fool wants it to say “Was Admired” on their tombstone.

Instead of competitive Navy Seal workouts, we need classes on how to connect authentically with other humans. And I'll give you a hint: it's not by comparing elite travel victories, handbags, or business cards à la "American Psycho."

Rather than teach people to optimize their physiques or pursue the kind of elective enhancement marketed to the wealthy as vitality, we should teach courses in the skills the Harvard study actually validates: having a sense of wonder, curiosity as a daily practice, active listening as a discipline, validating each other's emotional experiences, creating a balanced lifestyle, and choosing our words carefully. As Bruce Fink says, “Every speech act is a request for love.” Ditto for every social media post.

Yes, I live in a bizarrely beautiful and entertaining part of planet Earth, but if I had to find the most poetic way of describing the general feeling of the extreme California fitness and wellness craze, it would be "joyless decadence": engaging in outer and outward maxxing while feeling dead inside. Hoping that the latest and greatest trend will finally nourish our souls and give us the one thing we really crave: unconditional love.

But we've been duped. Happiness is an inside job. And competition and comparison are only fomenting more and more sad-sexy-rich people.

item.title: Healing Thyself: Managing Moral Injury in Healthcare
item.description:
Moral Injury

Healing Thyself: Managing Moral Injury in Healthcare

Diagnosing and treating feelings of moral distress in healthcare workers, on and off the job.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Making difficult healthcare decisions on behalf of patients can lead to perceptions of moral failure.
  • Moral distress and moral injury create ethical and clinical stressors for health care professionals.
  • Burdensome moral decisions are often made quickly in high-risk or emergency situations.

I have previously written about living with moral injury and reclaiming identity. This challenge is particularly acute among those who are charged with caring for the physical and mental well-being of others.

Healthcare professionals vicariously experience both success and failure as they participate in the decisions and consequences of sometimes life-and-death choices made by and on behalf of patients. This unique relationship with the individuals in their care can lead to perceptions of moral failure.

Although moral burden can often be managed by talking it through instead of remaining silent, the goal is to consider ways it can be prevented. Recent research may offer clues.

Source: Image by fernando zhiminaicela from Pixabay

The Evolution of Moral Distress and Moral Injury

Guixiang Yao et al. (2026) explored the concepts of moral distress and moral injury among health care professionals around the globe [i], recognizing both concepts as critical to understanding the clinical and ethical experiences of health care professionals. Conducting a nearly 20-year bibliometric analysis of moral distress and moral injury, examining 1,180 publications, they identified the main disciplinary foundations of their research as clinical medicine, nursing, psychology, and ethics.

Yao et al. identified moral distress as the dominant focus of research, with moral injury gaining increasing attention over the years, especially within high-intensity care settings and psychological outcomes.

Regarding the cause, they note that within contemporary health care practice, practitioners increasingly face settings that implicate professional values, complex moral judgment, and ethical duties. These experiences occur repeatedly in clinical and organizational settings, especially within contexts involving high-risk such as emergency or intensive care departments, pediatric or oncology services, or end-of-life care.

Yao et al. note that in these situations, health care professionals frequently accept moral responsibility for making decisions that involve outcomes including life-sustaining treatment or treatment withdrawal, as well as resource allocation, within the boundaries of policy or institutional constraints, resulting in profound feelings of moral conflict and burden.

Public Health Crises and Moral Burden

Yao et al. note that public health crises often magnify the experience of moral burden. A clear example of this occurred during the quick decisions heath care professionals were forced to make during the COVID-19 pandemic, operating under emergency directives, scarce resources, and competing interests of patients. Decisions made under these circumstances often produced outcomes that clashed with ethical and professional values and triggered moral distress and moral injury.

Yao et al. distinguish these morally distressing experiences from generalized occupational stress or feelings of emotional exhaustion because they stem from the perception of moral loss due to an inability to behave consistently with personal ethical values and meaning, rather than a heavy workload.

Moral Injury Diagnosis, Treatment, and Management

Unlike physical injury, moral injury can take years to heal—if it ever does. So for many healthcare professionals, the goal is emotional management.

Consistent with the personal experience of many, Yao et al. identified a growing concern with conflicting values, moral responsibility, and professional identity as health care providers. They acknowledge the contributing roles of organizational ethical climates and resource-related pressures within clinical contexts and conclude that both moral distress and moral injury should be regarded as institutionally related experiences as well as professional role expectations.

Regarding potential preventative measures, Yao et al. suggest that strengthening ethical assistance, improving communication, and developing a culture of support may help to preserve moral integrity and meaning. They also recognize the value of supplementing clinical and technical training with encouraging moral resilience, ethical reflection, organizational responsibility, and emphasizing meaning.

Sharing the Burden

Everyone on the front lines making monumental decisions should be assisted by organizational preventative measures and protocols to lessen the moral burden. Understanding the significant stressors involved in healthcare-related decisions is the first step towards cultivating a plan of action designed to lessen the moral burden on healthcare professionals, with the goal of assisting through collaborative, informed decision making.

item.title: Striking the Balance Between the Music and the Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

Striking the Balance Between the Music and the Therapy

What musical skill set is necessary to enter the music therapy field?

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • The field of music therapy encompasses multiple schools of thought, each possessing its own unique philosophy.
  • The philosophies yield different approaches as to how therapists leverage music to achieve therapeutic goals.
  • The various approaches lead to diverse ideas about the musical skill set required to enter the field.

Since I began writing my book, Music Between Your Ears, I’ve learned a great deal about the field of music therapy. I am grateful to Dr. Suzanne Sorel for recently expanding my understanding further. I heard her speak at a music therapy conference earlier this year. Afterward, I contacted her to ask if she would be willing to discuss how different philosophical approaches influence music therapy education. She graciously accepted my invitation.

Dr. Sorel relates that she was always interested in music while growing up, but her mother insisted she pursue a practical career if she wanted music to remain part of her life. Knowing she neither wanted to teach music nor live the life of a performer, she became a highly trained music therapist. She earned a doctor of arts (DA) degree and holds credentials as a licensed creative arts therapist (LCAT) and a board-certified music therapist (MT-BC). She also has decades of clinical experience. A professor at Molloy University, and passionate about preparing future music therapists, she established Molloy’s Graduate Music Therapy Program in 2008 and directed it through 2024.1 During that time, she taught and supervised hundreds of music therapists from the local, national, and international communities.

Music Therapists’ Relationships With Music

We began by discussing how music therapists orient their relationship with music. Dr. Sorel describes herself as a music-centered therapist.2 She explains, "If it makes musical sense, it makes clinical sense." Citing a colleague’s work, she adds, "Sometimes, it can be challenging to access our feelings in words. Music can be a powerful way to bypass blocks and experience true healing and newfound understanding."3

I then shared my perspective, which comes from caring for patients with neurological disorders for over 30 years. Whatever form of therapy is being practiced—physical, occupational, speech, or music—I believe its chief purpose is to improve a patient's functioning. That’s why, in my view, the patient care goals must be the focus. Music is the means by which a music therapist helps the patient achieve those goals.

Our subtly different starting points drove home to me the fact that music therapy encompasses several schools of thought, each with its own philosophy. As a neurologist, I became familiar with music therapy through neurologic music therapy, especially the work of Michael Thaut, Ph.D. Dr. Thaut, formerly a professor at Colorado State University, is now a professor at the University of Toronto. The music therapist who advised me while writing my book,4 Dwyer Conklin, trained under Dr. Thaut in Colorado.

Dr. Sorel relates that her approach is grounded in humanistic principles and focuses primarily on emotional and behavioral concerns. Her practice is rooted in the work of Paul Nordoff and Clive Robbins, particularly their pioneering explorations into the clinical use of improvised music.5 The Nordoff-Robbins approach to music therapy is based on the belief that every person possesses an innate responsiveness to music that can support personal growth and healing. Originally devised for children with developmental disabilities, this approach is now used with both children and adults in many different settings.

Keeping Music Therapy Education in Mind

What music skills are required to dream of a future in music therapy?
Source: PublicDomainPictures/Pixabay

Noting that her clients respond best when therapists take into account musical elements such as key, tone color (timbre), and volume (dynamics), Dr. Sorel believes that strong musicianship is the foundation of music therapy training. The graduate program she founded emphasizes piano and guitar skills—Dr. Sorel points out that this is consistent with accrediting requirements of the American Music Therapy Association—and prospective students must pass an audition in order to be admitted to the program.

This led us to discuss Dwyer Conklin's contribution to my book.6 His view is that music therapy programs can teach the musical skills students need after they are admitted. He argues that programs would do well to consider accepting students without music degrees because they can bring valuable knowledge and expertise from other fields, such as the biological sciences.

Dr. Sorel recognizes that music therapy programs may be isolating themselves by being housed within music departments. She is open to the idea that positioning music therapy more clearly as a health care profession could help bring it further into the mainstream of the healing arts.7 She also acknowledges that giving priority to piano and guitar may be too narrow a focus; for example, given the value of rhythm to music therapy, percussion skills might deserve greater recognition. Even so, she holds that strong musical ability remains an essential prerequisite for anyone seeking to enter music therapy training.

Wrap-Up

Our dialogue broadened my understanding of the field of music therapy and its diverse currents. Over the course of our conversation, I gained a deeper appreciation for another approach to music therapy and how its practitioners utilize music to achieve therapeutic goals. I also came away sensing that the question of how much—and what kind of—musical training should be required to enter a music therapy program will remain a topic of discussion within the profession.8

Thank you, Dr. Suzanne Sorel, for sharing your knowledge, experience, and insights with me.

item.title: Your Child’s Anxiety Has a Daily Schedule
item.description:
Anxiety

Your Child’s Anxiety Has a Daily Schedule

How a kid's worry changes from morning panic to bedtime spirals.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety often changes form as a child’s day unfolds.
  • Morning panic, after-school shutdowns, and bedtime spirals may share the same underlying worry cycle.
  • Targeting one predictable trouble spot can be more useful than trying to “fix anxiety” all day.

What if I share with you that anxiety in children can seem maddeningly unpredictable? After decades of working with anxious, overthinking children and teens, I’ve noticed something parents often miss: worry often follows the rhythms of a child’s day. The content changes, but the underlying pattern may not.

A child who appears fine at breakfast may unravel before school, shut down after dismissal, and suddenly have ten worries at bedtime. In this post, we'll look at morning, afternoon, and nighttime through the eyes of three kids (names have been changed for privacy) to illustrate anxiety's cyclical dynamic.

Morning: The 8-Year-Old Who Can’t Get Out the Door

Eight-year-old Elise is cheerful until it is time to leave. Suddenly she cannot find her water bottle. Then her shoe feels wrong. Then she needs to know whether her teacher will be there. On the surface, it looks like Elise has three separate problems. Often, it is one activated alarm system attaching itself to whatever is available. That is why arguing about the water bottle rarely helps, for parents.

As a child therapist, I believe the two most important skills to coach children on are calming down and problem-solving. A calmer response from parents, therefore, names what is happening (when you name it, you tame it): “Your worry alarm is loud this morning. Let’s handle one thing at a time.” The goal isn't a perfect morning, but helping the child move forward while worried.

Afternoon: The 12-Year-Old Who Says “Fine”

Twelve-year-old Jordan gets into the car after school and answers every question with “fine.” Twenty minutes later, he snaps at his younger brother over nothing. In this situation, Jordan's parents may assume the irritability is the problem. But after a day of social monitoring, academic demands, and holding himself together, Jordan may be depleted. Instead of interrogating him at pickup, his parent might say, “Good to see you. You don’t have to talk yet.” A snack, movement, music, or quiet may accomplish more than 10 questions. Sometimes the best anxiety intervention is creating room for a nervous system to come down.

This hour-by-hour pattern is also the framework behind my new book, 24 Hours to a Less Anxious Child: The One-Day Reset to Quiet Worry, Calm Overthinking, and Help Your Child Trust Themselves Again. In this article, and as I further explain in the book, anxiety usually isn't one problem that looks the same all day. It helps parents identify and intervene in moments when their child's worry tends to surface, offering a practical response for each.

Night: The 16-Year-Old Whose Brain Won’t Turn Off

Sixteen-year-old Ava manages school, activities, and friends all day. At 10:30 p.m., however, her mind becomes a courtroom with the prosecuting attorney saying, "You suck." Ava, for example, has thoughts that ramp up: Did I sound stupid? What if I fail the test? Why hasn’t she texted me back?

The complicating factor for Ava is that night removes the healthy distractions. The unfinished worries finally get the microphone and get amplified while children lie in bed, about to try to sleep. A parent who repeatedly supplies reassurance can accidentally become part of the loop. A better response may be: “I hear that your brain wants an answer tonight. Does this need solving now, or can we put it on tomorrow’s list?”

PACE Works Around the Clock

Coaching your child to learn to contain their worries, rather than getting mired in an incessant thought loop of seeking certainty, follows my Pace model for parents to help their child manage overthinking. I have written about this in other posts such as Raising Kids in a World That Rewards Anxiety. As a quick summary, when kids use the following (for worries at any time of the day or night), they learn to:

Pause by taking a gentle breath

Acknowledge their overthinking

Contain it by setting a boundary to stop stewing (write down the concern to address it later or tomorrow)

Engage in moving forward (in a task such as schoolwork, doing something fun, or getting ready for bed/reading)

By using this, the child's comfort remains, and their demand for certainty falls by the wayside.

Final Thought: Stop Treating Every Anxious Moment as a New Problem

Taken together, morning avoidance, after-school irritability, homework perfectionism, and bedtime rumination can look unrelated. They may actually be different expressions of the same overthinking cycle. That realization changes the parent’s job. Instead of chasing every worry, start noticing when anxiety reliably gets loud.

Pick one pressure point by reflecting on the examples I shared above. Change your response by adapting from the sample sound bites I presented, then observe what happens. My point is that a child doesn't need to become worry-free in 24 hours. But one day can reveal the pattern, and once parents see it, they have a much better chance of changing it.

item.title: Philosophical Swallows vs. Moles
item.description:
Philosophy

Philosophical Swallows vs. Moles

Philosophy’s divide: Dream about possibilities or get into the dirt of reality?

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • True philosophy must ground itself in reality, not untethered speculation.
  • Childlike philosophical wonder is valuable but doesn't replace mature, science-connected thinking.
  • Wild speculation has value but belongs in fiction rather than academic philosophy.

This is Part 2 in a two-part series on two very distinct styles of philosophy. Click here for Part 1.

Eric Schwitzgebel doesn’t want to “reserve the name of philosophy” for non-naturalistic philosophy. The swallows of philosophy have increasingly given up on that goal. However, the many swallows housed in philosophy departments do want to preserve the label philosophy for all “their fallacious attempts at superscientific knowledge.”

The Mole and the Swallow.
Source: AI-Generated

Like Machery, I respect Schwitzgebel, and I, too, agree that his writing makes for a mind-bending and enjoyable read. But I don’t think it is philosophy. It’s more akin to a science-fiction novel that bends the rules of reality, but shouldn’t be taken seriously as telling us anything about the actual world. Schwitzgebel, of course, is more than competent in doing actual philosophy, masterful even. He has frequently dealt in deeply naturalistic work, even conducting empirical research himself. And so he is a good foil here, since his case shows that swallows can become moles. While I think that philosophy has no need for swallows—indeed, that it must ‘purge’ itself of swallow-like flights of fancy to become respectable again—no one is prevented from becoming a mole and doing serious work.

Ironically, I did see some swallows today. I hope their reputation won’t be harmed by their association with wild speculation.

Machery’s metaphor is unfortunate, of course, for a multitude of reasons. After all, animals do not metamorphose into other species. I and many other philosophers are also animal lovers. How could anyone want to get rid of swallows? Don’t we want a diverse ecosystem? Furthermore, given the choice between being a swallow soaring through the skies or a mole burrowing in the dirt, philosophers uninterested in finding themselves constrained by science will feel themselves vindicated. Swallows are free. They can explore the whole world, whereas moles can only ever explore parts of it. Worse, moles have poor vision. So it might be read as a kind of self-own of Machery to describe himself as a mole.

But there is a better way we can think of the difference between moles and swallows here, and it is ironically one provided by Schwitzgebel himself in the final paragraph of his book:

Childlike philosophy toys with wild ideas at the boundaries of our understanding. Wild theorizing about consciousness is common. But are these ideas useful or true? Can we plug them in straightaway into our existing conceptions and put them to work? For me, if I was already sure they were false and useless, that would steal away their charm. But to be in a hurry to judge their merits, to want to expunge doubt and wonder so as to settle on a final view that we can put immediately to work, to want to close rather than open—let’s not be in such a rush to grow up. What’s life for if there’s no time to play and explore? –Eric Schwitzgebel

Rather than thinking about the two kinds of philosophers as swallows and moles, I believe it is more useful to think of them as placed at different stages in the maturity of philosophical development. Children and adults. Childlike and mature philosophy. Or in Reichenbach’s terminology, the ‘speculative philosophy’ of the past and the ‘scientific philosophy’ of the future.

Children engage in wild speculation entirely untethered from the knowledge humanity has accumulated. Even logic is thrown out of the window. As adults, we look at their innocence and curiosity with nothing but encouragement and love. But if an adult fails to distinguish imagination from reality, the only response left is pity. Childlike philosophy is but one step in one’s development as a philosopher. But eventually it is time to grow up.

Earlier in his book, Schwitzgebel writes: “It would just be too sad if the world had no space for speculation about wild hypotheticals.” Sad that may be. But no one is trying to ban wild speculations. They are just no longer viewed as philosophy and should thus be confined to the fiction sections of bookstores. They can still make for an enjoyable read and even hit bestseller lists nonetheless. Mature philosophy is also not against all speculation or diversity either. Science is filled with speculations that are motivated by what we have learned. Science is filled with bizarre and unintuitive conclusions because intuitions and common sense play little to no role in the search for truth. But what would be a truly sad and pitiful state of affairs is if “wild” speculations entirely unconnected from the sciences were continued to be viewed as serious philosophy within the field. For it would justifiably lead to the continued decline in the respect philosophers once held. It would undermine the status of philosophy as a serious academic field in search of truth.

If we are keen to experience the weird, diverse, and wonderful, one has to look no further than to the actual world.

item.title: Moral Sensitivity and Speaking Up Makes You the Problem
item.description:
Highly Sensitive Person

Moral Sensitivity and Speaking Up Makes You the Problem

You may be the morally sensitive canary that no one thanks.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Moral sensitivity means noticing the ethical weight of a situation quickly and profoundly..
  • The pain of being a morally sensitive person is caused by the silence of everyone else.
  • With moral sensitivity, what is missing is the person who sees what you see and is willing to say it out loud.
  • We cannot change how much you do see, the only thing under your control is where you spend energy.

Having heightened moral sensitivity means noticing the ethical weight of a situation more quickly and more penetratively than most people do. For some, it also means that witnessing injustice hurts more. Perhaps you saw somebody being spoken to with contempt disguised as banter, or someone who cannot afford to complain being treated badly. You cannot help but see it, and hours later, sometimes days later, you are still churning it over, while most of the people around you either did not see it or dropped it long ago.

Values you hold dear have been violated, whether it is fairness, honesty, kindness, or the ordinary decency people owe each other. The unease of having seen something wrong and being unable to do anything about it lodges in you and will not settle until something is done.

All of that is painful in itself, and what hurts more is looking around and finding that nobody else wants to speak up. The pain of being a morally sensitive person is not just caused by the wrongdoing you see. It is caused by the silence of everyone else who saw it, and by what happens to you when you break that silence.

When you were younger and unaware of your heightened moral sensitivity, you thought everybody worked the way you did. You assumed that people minded fairness, that they saw what you saw, that they were as bothered as you were. You may even have assumed people would thank you for pointing out what needed changing, because surely everybody in the room enjoyed the relief. It took years for you to realise that when you do speak up, you sometimes get framed as the problematic one.

The Manifestations of Moral Outrage

Moral sensitivity is not only a matter of intellectual judgment. Rage against immorality finds its way into your body. There is heat in the face, tightness in the chest, the throat closing slightly, a jolt of something that is not quite anger and not quite fear. Your body tells you that something you care about has been violated before you have had any say in the matter.

People with heightened moral sensitivity can be likened to canaries in the coal mine. Miners took the bird down with them because the gas would reach it long before any of them felt anything, and its collapse was the warning that got everybody else out alive. Perhaps you are that canary. Moral sensitivity is a warning system that says something is wrong.

People have come to rely on you. Once a group has learned that you are the one who would be the spokesperson, the changemaker, nobody else has to spend awareness or energy being the guardian of justice, because they already know you will mention it. They carry no risk, and they get the improvement anyway. Moral sensitivity turns out to be a resource other people can use without ever acknowledging that they are using it. But you cannot name it because none of this is arranged deliberately. Nobody in the room has cast you in that role, or collectively decided that you will be the designated conscience.

After being the canary for a while, the role sometimes turns on you. You are the one who made the fuss. You become framed as the sensitive one, the intense one, the one who cannot leave things alone. What is worse is that after enough repetitions you start to internalise the accusation. You wonder whether they were right, whether you are too sensitive, too pedantic, too much trouble to have around. What was moral sensitivity begins to look like a defect of character. You begin editing yourself before you speak, running your own perception past an internal committee to check whether it is proportionate.

The Mischaracterizations of Moral Sensitivity

People assume that the compulsion to say something is a preference, that you are choosing to have high standards, to be difficult, to be dissatisfied with the world. Even your therapist does not always get it. They try to work with you on relinquishing unrealistic standards, and you sit there unable to explain that what they call a high standard does not feel like a standard at all. It feels like the minimum standard, what people do when they have basic human decency. It is not that you require people to be exceptional. It is that you cannot pretend not to have noticed when they are not even being ordinarily decent.

Being a canary is deeply lonely. You can have a partner, colleagues, a full house, and still feel deeply alone. With moral sensitivity, what is missing is not physical company. What is missing is one person who sees what you see and is willing to say it out loud. Reality is meant to be a thing people hold between them. But your version of reality is never confirmed. When something affects you, there is no one to confirm it and say, 'Yes, that happened; I saw it too.'

Perhaps there is grief under the anger and rage against injustice. You are mourning the version of things that would have existed if people had behaved the way they were capable of. Perhaps the rage is what keeps the sense of possibility open. If you were to take away the rage and fully reconcile with how little people change, a deep sadness would set in, and possibly something closer to despair. In a way, the rage keeps you safe from the despair.

We cannot ask you not to see, not to feel, or to turn a blind eye. But carrying the weight of the world on your shoulders is not sustainable, and the guilt of not being able to do more is eating you up and serving no one. However, you may be able to change how much of it you carry. We cannot change how much you do see; the only thing under your control is where you spend yourself. You cannot change a person who has no intention of being changed. Nobody can attempt to fix every wrong they see in the world and also have a life. Choosing which things to take up is not a betrayal of anything you believe; it is wisdom.

You can grieve what people are and still want better from them. And you can stop for the world to change, and instead choose to walk away from corruption. You may go on being misunderstood, and the gratitude for your truth-telling may go on being missing. What you can always hold on to is that you honoured your own knowledge of what you saw and what you did about it, and you know you have not betrayed who you are.

item.title: An Eye-Opening Discussion on How Insects Make Us Human
item.description:
Philosophy

An Eye-Opening Discussion on How Insects Make Us Human

Boria Sax explains how insects help us understand identity and extinction.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Dr. Boria Sax's new book is "The Butterfly Who Dreamt He Was a Man: Metamorphoses, Entomological and Human."
  • Sax offers a cultural and philosophical journey that shows why losing insects means losing part of ourselves.
  • The root of the word “psychology” is psychê, which in Greek means both “soul” and “butterfly.”
Source: ANKIT BHATTACHERJEE/Pexels

Insects are amazing animals. It always baffles me how a single word can be used to refer to the astounding—unimaginable—diversity of around 10 quintillion (18 zeros after the number 10) beings who belong to around 5.5 million species who occupy our planet.

I don't know all that much about the vast majority of these animals but I am greatly attracted to butterflies and bees, so when I learned of Dr. Boria Sax's new book The Butterfly Who Dreamt He Was a Man: Metamorphoses, Entomological and Human, I couldn't wait to get my eyes on it. Now that I have, I was pleased he could answer a few questions about his landmark book in which he "offers an imaginative lens on the growing crisis of insect extinction ... a cultural and philosophical journey that shows why losing insects means losing part of ourselves." Here's what he had to say about his highly original book.

Marc Bekoff: Why would readers of Psychology Today be interested in your book?

Boria Sax: In The Butterfly Who Dreamt He was a Man, I write about how stories are the major way in which people organize experience. From the Neolithic forager in a forest to a contemporary teenager surfing the Internet, people have always been surrounded by more items clamoring for attention than they can even notice. Stories tell us what merits special attention and what should be ignored. They divide experience into units that can teach practical or moral lessons.

Each of us is a collection of stories, far more than he or she can tell or even know. But the person who is aware of his or her own stories will be more grounded and better able to articulate priorities. Insects have provided major templates for our stories. Their lives, like ours, are divided into phases, analogous to youth and adulthood, which are marked by the shedding of an exoskeleton. Many insects such as cicadas and butterflies undergo a final, dramatic metamorphosis, which is the culmination of their lives.

The root of the word “psychology” is psychê, which in Greek means both “soul” and “butterfly.” The idea of the soul as a butterfly is found in indigenous cultures on every continent except Antarctica. In Mexico, the Day of the Dead coincides with the arrival of migrating monarch butterflies. Among the most beloved folktales in China for well over a thousand years is that of the Butterfly Lovers, a young man and woman who were separated when the girl’s parents arranged for her to have a political marriage. The young man died and the young woman jumped into his grave, after which the two emerged as butterflies. Early entomologists such as Johannes Goedaert and Maria Sibylla Merian were devout Protestants who believed that the study of butterflies would help them understand the mystery of resurrection. Insects are familiar enough to be taken for granted most of the time, but, when you stop to think about them, strange enough to challenge our conventional perspectives on the world.

MB: Why did you write The Butterfly Who Dreamt He was a Man?

BS: Throughout my academic career, I have constantly pushed the limits of what was acceptable in scholarly work by including storytelling, humor, and lyricism alongside academic argument. This has at times led to indignant rejections of my work, though it has not stopped me from publishing about 20 books and scores of articles. In this book, in many ways, I carry this further than ever before.

Source: Reaction Book, used with permission

The Daoist philosopher Zhuang Zhou told how he had dreamed of being a butterfly. On waking, he asked whether that was really a dream. Or was he, perhaps, a butterfly dreaming of being a man? I ask the reader to imagine an academic conference, set up using the newly discovered art of time travel, devoted to that question. Among those invited are a Native Australian, a Native American, a late Renaissance philosopher, and so on. Also present are Emily Dickinson, Maria Sibylla Merian, Franz Kafka, Albrecht Dürer, and many others. Finally, Zhuang Zhou himself appears at the end. But this is only a fictional frame for my realistic discussion, which covers the cultural history, symbolism, study, and artistic representation of insects.

At times, my style may have become a way of indirectly addressing themes that were too elusive, emotionally charged, complicated, or repressed to tackle directly. In my latest book, I have tried to increase my scope by articulating a larger range of perspectives. In summary, this book is a culmination of endeavors that I have been working on for most of my life.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of the major messages?

BS: In the words of psychologist James Hillman, “Nothing equals our murderous passion to eradicate insect pests.” Countless movies from the 1950s featured giant insects carrying off screaming young women. Meanwhile, advertisements for insect poisons depicted flies and mosquitoes as vicious criminals, so that people could enjoy killing them as revenge. This fury at insects has led to their massive disappearance, which now extends not only to cities but even remote areas of Amazonia. It deprives birds of food and plants of pollination, to a point where it is a major threat to the environment.

The rage can also be transferred to other human beings, and people have often spoken of their enemies as “pests, “flies,” or “vermin.” Zyklon B, the gas used by the Nazis to kill people in concentration camps, was first developed as an insecticide. I conclude my introduction with the words:

"My role here is to show how people relate to insects with the same intimacy as they do to mammals but in profoundly different ways. They not only share our lives but our story as well. Insects are also an essential part of the natural environment and human culture, to a point where, without small invertebrates, we could not be very human at all."

Mammals generally go through a brief childhood, but their lives are lived mostly on the single level of maturity. Insects, by contrast, repeatedly cast off their external covering and undergo metamorphoses such as that of a caterpillar to a chrysalis and, finally, a butterfly. These transformations provide models for our division of human life into stages such as infancy, childhood, adolescence, maturity, old age, and death.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

BS: My book does not target any particular demographic. I want to reach people as individuals, a goal that is notoriously quirky and unpredictable. If my writings can be deeply meaningful to a few people, that means a lot to me. Beyond that, I also hope that my ideas will be discussed, not only in academia but also in libraries, coffee houses, pubs, chatrooms, and wherever people get together.

item.title: A Novel Benefit of the Psychedelic Ibogaine
item.description:
Psychedelics

A Novel Benefit of the Psychedelic Ibogaine

Plant-based psychedelics may offer hope for the treatment of brain disorders.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • Ibogaine is recognized for its well-established anti-addictive properties.
  • Ibogaine may also facilitate improved clinical outcomes in MS and opioid use disorder.
  • Specifically, ibogaine upregulates protein and gene expression, leading to the remyelination of white matter.

Ibogaine is the primary alkaloid in Tabernanthe iboga root bark. It’s a perennial plant native to the tropical rainforests of West Central Africa. It has been used in traditional African medicine for centuries. It induces profound mental, emotional, and spiritual experiences. In the West, it has been more recently recognized for its well-established anti-addictive properties. Numerous studies link ibogaine administration with reductions in drug cravings, in symptoms of withdrawal, and in return to opioid use (Barsuglia et al., 2018; Mash, 2023). The benefits it offers to reduce opioid addiction are likely related to the complex actions of ibogaine at the brain’s opioid receptors.

Ibogaine has truly revolutionized the treatment of opioid addiction. Multiple open-label trials of hundreds of patients have discovered that a single dose administration of ibogaine reduced the use of prescription opioids and heroin. A single administration of ibogaine reduced opioid craving, insomnia, and depressed mood for several weeks after treatment. Ibogaine also reduced the major symptoms of opioid withdrawal.

What Other Conditions Might Ibogaine Treat?

Some recent studies suggest that ibogaine might also reduce the symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder, multiple sclerosis (MS), neuropathic pain disorder, traumatic brain injury, and Parkinson’s disease. I know that such a broad list of potential effects suggests that ibogaine is too good to be true. Ibogaines beneficial effects, if they can be substantiated, might be explained by the ability of ibogaine to act on so many different neurotransmitter systems in the brain, including glutamate, serotonin, Sigma receptors, and acetylcholine nicotinic receptors.

A recent article focused on the potential mechanisms that allow ibogaine to facilitate remyelination and lead to improved clinical outcomes in MS and opioid use disorder.

Recent research has discovered that ibogaine can upregulate protein and gene expression in MS patients leading to the remyelination of white matter as well as facilitate its repair. Patients with MS lose their white matter, which is called a myelin sheath and is made by specialized cells in the brain. The loss of the myelin sheath around axons underlies the array of symptoms associated with MS. The loss of the myelin sheath leads to the failure of some nerve fibers throughout the brain and body to carry electrical signals to their targets. The absence of electrical signals in vulnerable pathways causes MS patients to suffer with clumsiness, loss of balance and coordination, difficulty with cognitive function, muscle stiffness and muscle spasm, and vision changes.

Opioids are particularly harmful to the white matter in the brain. Chronic opioid administration reduces the levels of proteins that are critical to the health of myelin. In humans, the extent of white matter damage worsens with an increase in the duration of exposure to opioids. Unfortunately, any opioid is capable of producing damage—even methadone, which is used during most addiction recovery therapies. Long-term heroin use produces a spongiform degeneration of white matter characterized by large vacuoles and axonal spheroids that indicate the loss of myelin, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes.

In Summary

Numerous clinical trials indicate that ibogaine can upregulate markers of myelination under conditions of both opioid use disorder or MS. Ibogaine’s ability to produce these beneficial changes in the brain depend upon its complex actions at multiple neurotransmitter receptors. These complex actions reduce the glutamate toxicity and correct some metabolic processes leading to long-lasting neuroplasticity that facilitates neuronal repair and remyelination. Ibogaine joins a growing list of psychedelic drugs that have been discovered to potentially produce beneficial effects on brain health and mood.
